readings.title: This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison
readings.challenge: Follow a speaker who describes a walk he is not on, and find the line where his complaint turns.
readings.focus: Imagination and sympathy as a way of sharing what one has lost.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). The lime here is the linden tree, not the citrus fruit; a bower is a shady garden shelter. Charles Lamb, later a famous essayist, was Coleridge’s school friend; he worked as a clerk in the East India Company’s London offices and had suffered a terrible family tragedy the year before. A dell is a small wooded valley; a bark is a ship; the “many-steepled tract” is country with many church towers; a rook is a large crow.

excerpt.locator: This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison, the whole poem with its dedication, Coleridge’s headnote and date; opens “[ADDRESSED TO CHARLES LAMB, OF THE INDIA HOUSE, LONDON]”; closes “1797.”.

questions.prompt: In the first stanza the speaker describes a place he cannot see. How does he manage it, and what does it show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers the dell and pictures his friends reaching it, down to the ash tree’s leaves and the dripping weeds. His imagination goes on the walk without him; “of which I told” suggests he planned the route for them, so even his complaint is generous.
evidence: To that still roaring dell, of which I told;
Still nod and drip beneath the dripping edge

questions.prompt: Why does he imagine Charles as the gladdest of the walkers?
facilitatorNotes: Lamb has been shut up in London for years and has suffered; the countryside means most to someone deprived of it. The speaker then commands the sun, flowers and clouds to shine for his friend, as if staging the sunset for him.
evidence: And hunger'd after Nature, many a year, In the great City pent,

questions.prompt: Where does the poem turn, and what does the speaker find in his “prison”?
facilitatorNotes: At “A delight / Comes sudden on my heart”: sharing his friends’ joy in imagination makes him glad, and he notices his own small bower: leaf shadows, the walnut, ivy, the bat and the humble-bee. The prison becomes enough.
evidence: A delight Comes sudden on my heart, and I am glad As I myself were there!
No plot so narrow, be but Nature there,

questions.prompt: “'Tis well to be bereft of promis'd good.” Do you agree? How does the rook at the end join the two friends?
facilitatorNotes: He argues that losing a pleasure can teach us to enjoy others’ joys. The single rook flying home may cross both men’s sight, linking the bower and the hill. Some readers find the consolation earned; others think it a little too neat, a way of talking himself out of disappointment.
evidence: 'Tis well to be bereft of promis'd good,
Homewards, I blest it!

readings.title: Christabel, Part I: the lady under the oak
readings.challenge: Listen for the questions the narrator asks, and notice which ones he answers.
readings.focus: A Gothic ballad builds suspense from small wrong notes.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). Coleridge began Christabel in 1797, wrote its second part in 1800, and published both in 1816; he never finished it. In his preface he explains that each line has four stressed beats, though the number of syllables changes. A mastiff is a large guard dog (a bitch is a female); weal is welfare; misletoe is mistletoe; a palfrey is a gentle riding horse; “I wis” means “I know” or “surely”; “amain” is at full speed; chivalry here means knights.
readings.contentNote: Geraldine says that armed men seized her and carried her off; the scene is meant to frighten.

excerpt.locator: Christabel, Part I, from the opening to the crossing of the castle court; opens “'Tis the middle of night by the castle clock, And the owls have awakened the crowing…”; closes “…So free from danger, free from fear, They crossed the court: right glad they were.”.

questions.prompt: The poem opens with sounds at midnight. Which of them seem wrong or out of place, and how do they set the mood?
facilitatorNotes: The owls wake the cock, which crows at midnight instead of dawn; the old dog howls sixteen times, as if counting the clock; and some say she sees the dead lady’s shroud. Nothing is openly supernatural yet, but the ordinary world is slightly off.
evidence: And the owls have awakened the crowing cock;
Some say, she sees my lady's shroud.

questions.prompt: “Is the night chilly and dark? / The night is chilly, but not dark.” Who seems to ask and who answers? How does this way of telling build suspense?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator questions himself like a ballad-singer talking to listeners, then answers, correcting the expected word. The questions slow the story at the key moment (“What sees she there?”) and draw us in as if we were present.
evidence: Is the night chilly and dark?
What sees she there?

questions.prompt: What is strange about Geraldine, beyond her beauty? Look at her story and at how she enters the castle.
facilitatorNotes: She cannot say who the men were or how long she lay there; at the gate she sinks and must be lifted over the threshold, then walks “as she were not in pain.” In many old tales an evil spirit cannot enter a house unless it is carried or invited in. When Christabel praises the Virgin, Geraldine says she is too weary to speak.
evidence: Lifted her up, a weary weight, Over the threshold of the gate:
Alas, alas! said Geraldine, I cannot speak for weariness.

questions.prompt: Christabel helps at every step. Is the poem simply praising her goodness, or also showing a danger in innocence?
facilitatorNotes: Her charity is real: she comforts, promises her father’s protection and offers her own bed. But each kindness opens the castle further to someone she cannot read. Readers may admire her, pity her, or see both at once.
evidence: Then Christabel stretched forth her hand, And comforted fair Geraldine:
This night, to share your couch with me.

readings.title: Christabel, Part I: the spell
readings.challenge: Collect the signs that something is wrong, and notice what the narrator refuses to describe.
readings.focus: Suspense created by what is withheld.
readings.context: Recap: praying in the woods at midnight, Christabel found Geraldine, a richly dressed lady who said warriors had carried her off. Christabel brought her secretly into her father’s castle, lifting her over the threshold. Brands are burning logs; the boss is the raised centre of a shield; rushes were strewn on floors; a cordial is a strengthening drink; “peak and pine” means waste away; a cincture is a belt and a vest a garment; “wel-a-day” means alas.
readings.contentNote: Geraldine undresses and takes Christabel in her arms, casting a spell. The poem never says what Christabel sees, only that it is “a sight to dream of, not to tell.”

excerpt.locator: Christabel, Part I, from the sleeping mastiff to the end of Part I; opens “Outside her kennel, the mastiff old Lay fast asleep, in moonshine cold. The mastiff old…”; closes “…home with thee in love and in charity, To shield her and shelter her from the damp air.'”.

questions.prompt: As Geraldine passes, the old mastiff moans and the dying fire flares. What do these signs suggest, and why does the narrator offer an ordinary explanation for the first?
facilitatorNotes: Animals and fire react to something unnatural. The narrator’s “Perhaps it is the owlet’s scritch” seems to explain the moan away, but repeating “what can ail the mastiff” keeps us suspicious.
evidence: Yet she an angry moan did make!
Perhaps it is the owlet's scritch:
A tongue of light, a fit of flame;

questions.prompt: When Christabel wishes her dead mother were there, Geraldine speaks in an “altered voice.” Whom is she speaking to, and what does it reveal?
facilitatorNotes: To the mother’s spirit, which she calls Christabel’s “guardian,” and which she claims the power to drive away. It is the clearest sign that she is a supernatural enemy. Christabel explains it away as the effect of the “ghastly ride.”
evidence: 'Off, wandering mother! Peak and pine! I have power to bid thee flee.'
Though thou her guardian spirit be,

questions.prompt: “A sight to dream of, not to tell!” Why might the poem refuse to show what Christabel sees? Does the gap make the moment more or less frightening?
facilitatorNotes: Leaving it unsaid lets readers imagine the worst and keeps Geraldine mysterious; Part II will add only that the bosom is “old” and “cold.” Some readers find the silence powerful, others frustrating; both are worth arguing from the text.
evidence: Behold! her bosom and half her side--
A sight to dream of, not to tell!

questions.prompt: What exactly does Geraldine’s spell do, and why is it especially cruel?
facilitatorNotes: It masters Christabel’s speech: she can tell only that she heard a moaning, found a lady and brought her home “in love and in charity.” Her own kindness becomes the only story she is allowed to tell, so her virtue is used to silence her.
evidence: Which is lord of thy utterance, Christabel!
And didst bring her home with thee in love and in charity,

readings.title: Christabel, Parts I–II: morning in the Baron’s hall
readings.challenge: Watch how the narrator’s comforting words sit beside what he shows, and notice who knows what in the hall.
readings.focus: Dramatic irony: the reader sees the danger that Christabel cannot name and her father cannot see.
readings.context: Recap: Christabel brought a stranger, Geraldine, into her bedroom; Geraldine undressed, showing something terrible, and took her in her arms under a spell, so that Christabel can say only that she found a lady in the woods and brought her home. Bale is harm; a tairn (tarn) is a mountain lake, a rill a stream and a fell a hill; the matin bell rings for morning prayers and the sacristan rings it, counting prayers on beads between strokes; Bratha Head, Wyndermere, Langdale and Borodale are places in the Lake District, where Part II is set; to be wroth is to be angry; “kenned” means recognised; recreant means cowardly.

excerpt.locator: Christabel, the Conclusion to Part I with its date and Part II to Christabel’s “All will yet be well!”; opens “It was a lovely sight to see The lady Christabel, when she Was praying at the old oak…”; closes “…will yet be well!' I ween, she had no power to tell Aught else: so mighty was the spell.”.

questions.prompt: The Conclusion to Part I says Geraldine holds Christabel “As a mother with her child.” Why is the comparison disturbing here?
facilitatorNotes: Christabel’s mother is dead and her guardian spirit was just driven off; now “the worker of these harms” takes the mother’s place. The tender image hides a prison (“arms of thine / Have been the lovely lady’s prison”).
evidence: As a mother with her child.
And lo! the worker of these harms,

questions.prompt: The Conclusion ends, “For the blue sky bends over all!” Is the comfort convincing after what we have seen?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator insists that saints help those who call and that Christabel may be dreaming of her mother. Some readers take it as real hope; others hear a narrator talking himself into it (“No doubt, she hath a vision sweet”), where “No doubt” raises doubt.
evidence: No doubt, she hath a vision sweet.
For the blue sky bends over all!

questions.prompt: Why does Sir Leoline turn pale at Lord Roland’s name? What does the passage say about anger between friends?
facilitatorNotes: Roland was his dearest friend until “whispering tongues” set them against each other. Anger at someone we love works “like madness,” and the break leaves scars like cliffs split by the sea. Welcoming Roland’s daughter lets him hope to mend it, which is exactly the feeling Geraldine uses.
evidence: And to be wroth with one we love Doth work like madness in the brain.
Like cliffs which had been rent asunder;

questions.prompt: When her father embraces Geraldine, Christabel hisses and then says only “All will yet be well!” How must she appear to him?
facilitatorNotes: He turns and sees only his daughter praying, then hears a cheerful answer that explains nothing. The spell lets her say nothing true. The reader knows why she shudders; her father does not, and that gap is the source of the coming trouble.
evidence: And drew in her breath with a hissing sound:
Made answer, 'All will yet be well!'

readings.title: Christabel, Part II: Bracy’s dream
readings.challenge: Interpret a dream that the characters misread, and decide what the unfinished poem leaves open.
readings.focus: How a spell turns innocence into the look of guilt.
readings.context: Recap: Geraldine has bewitched Christabel so that she cannot tell what she saw, and has charmed Sir Leoline, who recognises her as the daughter of Lord Roland, the friend he quarrelled with long ago. The Irthing is a river near the border with Scotland; a bard is a poet and musician; a boon is a favour; “askance” means sideways, with suspicion; “inly” means inwardly. Coleridge never wrote the rest of the poem; the Conclusion to Part II was written separately and printed with it.

excerpt.locator: Christabel, Part II from Geraldine’s request to go home to its end, with the Conclusion to Part II and the dates; opens “Yet he, who saw this Geraldine, Had deemed her sure a thing divine: Such sorrow with such…”; closes “1801.”.

questions.prompt: What does Bracy dream, and how does Sir Leoline apply the dream?
facilitatorNotes: Bracy sees the dove named after Christabel trapped by a green snake coiled round its neck: plainly Geraldine and Christabel. Sir Leoline calls Geraldine “Lord Roland’s beauteous dove” and promises to crush the snake, reversing the meaning. The reader sees the irony at once.
evidence: When lo! I saw a bright green snake Coiled around its wings and neck.
Thy sire and I will crush the snake!

questions.prompt: Christabel copies Geraldine’s serpent look “With forced unconscious sympathy.” What happens to her, and why does it matter that it happens “Full before her father’s view”?
facilitatorNotes: Her innocent face takes on a look of “dull and treacherous hate,” and her father sees it. The spell makes the victim look like the villain at the worst moment.
evidence: And passively did imitate That look of dull and treacherous hate!
Full before her father's view----

questions.prompt: Why does Sir Leoline side with Geraldine against his daughter? Is he only deceived, or does his character play a part?
facilitatorNotes: He is deceived, but pride and rage do the rest: he feels “Dishonoured” and blames “more than woman’s jealousy.” The narrator even pleads with him to remember the mother’s prayer. Readers may judge him harshly or pity a man trapped by his own feelings.
evidence: Dishonoured thus in his old age;
By more than woman's jealousy

questions.prompt: The Conclusion to Part II describes a father who speaks “words of unmeant bitterness” to a child he loves. How might it connect to the poem, and what does its ending suggest?
facilitatorNotes: It may comment on Sir Leoline’s harsh words, or on any loving parent who speaks bitterly. Its last lines suggest that such words usually come “from rage and pain.” Because the poem is unfinished, readers must decide how the pieces fit.
evidence: With words of unmeant bitterness.
Comes seldom save from rage and pain,

readings.title: Frost at Midnight
readings.challenge: Follow the poem from the silent room to memory, to a hoped-for future, and back.
readings.focus: A father’s meditation turns a silent winter night into a blessing for his child.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). He wrote this in February 1798 beside his baby son, Hartley. The “film” on the grate is a flake of soot; in folklore it was called a “stranger” and foretold an unexpected visitor. As a boy Coleridge was sent to a London boarding school (the “preceptor” is a teacher) and missed his home in Devon. “Pent” means shut in; the “sister more beloved” and he were dressed alike as small children. “Intersperséd vacancies” are scattered pauses.

excerpt.locator: Frost at Midnight, the whole poem with its date; opens “The Frost performs its secret ministry, Unhelped by any wind. The owlet's cry Came…”; closes “_February_, 1798.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the calm “disturb” the speaker? What is “the sole unquiet thing,” and what does his mind do with it?
facilitatorNotes: The silence is so complete that it vexes him. The fluttering film becomes a companion, because the idle mind looks everywhere for an “echo or mirror” of itself. He admits that this makes “a toy of Thought.”
evidence: 'Tis calm indeed! so calm that it disturbs
Still flutters there, the sole unquiet thing.

questions.prompt: How does the film on the grate lead him back to his schooldays? What did the boy hope for?
facilitatorNotes: The same superstition made him watch the grate at school, dreaming of his birthplace and its bells, and then watch the classroom door all morning for a visitor from home. The memory shows a lonely child in a strict city school.
evidence: Awed by the stern preceptor's face, mine eye Fixed with mock study on my swimming book:
My play-mate when we both were clothed alike!

questions.prompt: What different childhood does he promise his son, and what does he think nature will teach?
facilitatorNotes: The baby will wander among lakes, shores and mountains instead of city cloisters, and learn from nature as from “that eternal language” in which God teaches. The poem treats landscape as a teacher that makes the spirit “ask.”
evidence: shalt wander like a breeze By lakes and sandy shores
Of that eternal language, which thy God Utters,

questions.prompt: The poem ends with “the secret ministry of frost,” as it began. What has changed by the time we return to it?
facilitatorNotes: At the start the frost works unseen while the speaker feels uneasy; at the end it hangs icicles “Quietly shining to the quiet Moon,” part of a calm blessing. The circular shape lets the same night feel different after the journey through memory and hope.
evidence: The Frost performs its secret ministry,
Quietly shining to the quiet Moon.

readings.title: The Nightingale
readings.challenge: Follow an argument made in the relaxed voice of someone talking to friends on an evening walk.
readings.focus: Whether we hear nature as it is or fill it with our own feelings.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). The “Friend” and “Sister” are William Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy. “Most musical, most melancholy” is a line from Milton’s poem Il Penseroso; in Greek myth Philomela was turned into a nightingale after a terrible wrong, so poets long called the bird’s song sad. “Jug jug” imitates the song; king-cups are buttercups or marsh marigolds; a glow-worm is a beetle whose female gives off light; the babe is Coleridge’s son Hartley.

excerpt.locator: The Nightingale: A Conversation Poem, April, 1798, the whole poem with its date; opens “No cloud, no relique of the sunken day Distinguishes the West, no long thin slip Of…”; closes “1798.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker reject calling the nightingale “melancholy”? Who, according to him, gave the bird that reputation?
facilitatorNotes: A sorrowing man who “filled all things with himself” heard his own grief in the song, and poets copied him. The speaker’s point is that the sadness belonged to the listener, not the bird.
evidence: In Nature there is nothing melancholy.
(And so, poor wretch! filled all things with himself,

questions.prompt: What does he think a poet should do instead of “building up the rhyme”? Is there an irony in saying this in a poem?
facilitatorNotes: Lie by a brook and surrender to the shapes and sounds around him, forgetting fame; then his song would be loved like nature. The irony is that this is a poem, though its loose, talking blank verse tries to sound like an evening conversation rather than a performance.
evidence: Surrendering his whole spirit, of his song And of his fame forgetful!

questions.prompt: Which words in the passages about the grove and the gentle Maid make the birds’ singing sound joyful and lively?
facilitatorNotes: They “answer and provoke each other,” skirmish, burst forth like “a hundred airy harps,” and one sings “Like tipsy Joy that reels with tossing head.” The language is quick, crowded and merry, the opposite of a lament.
evidence: They answer and provoke each other's song,
Like tipsy Joy that reels with tossing head.

questions.prompt: Why does the poem end with the baby and the moon? How does the story support the argument about nightingales?
facilitatorNotes: The crying child is soothed by the moon and laughs, so the father wants him to grow up linking night with joy. It is his own small proof, though he admits “It is a father’s tale.” Readers may find it moving or decide it proves only what the father hopes.
evidence: And I deem it wise To make him Nature's play-mate.
He may associate joy.

readings.title: The Eolian Harp
readings.challenge: Follow a poem that drifts from a quiet evening into a daring idea, and then draws back from it.
readings.focus: The wind harp as an image of the mind and of nature, and a speaker who retreats from his own speculation.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). He wrote this in 1795 (the date is printed at the end) at Clevedon on the Somerset coast, soon after marrying Sara Fricker. An Eolian or Aeolian harp, named after Aeolus, the Greek god of the winds, is a wooden box strung with strings that sound when the wind blows across them; it was laid in an open window, or casement. A cot is a cottage; “desultory” means wandering at random; “sequacious” means following one after another; “plastic” here means shaping; “the main” is the sea; “unregenerate” means not yet spiritually renewed.

excerpt.locator: The Eolian Harp, composed at Clevedon, Somersetshire, the whole poem with its date; opens “My pensive Sara! thy soft cheek reclined Thus on mine arm, most soothing sweet it is To…”; closes “1795.”.

questions.prompt: Which details make the opening evening feel hushed? What is odd about saying that the murmur of the sea “Tells us of silence”?
facilitatorNotes: Sara’s cheek on his arm, clouds “Slow saddening,” the evening star, the scent from the bean-field. The sea’s faint sound makes the silence noticeable: we hear how quiet it is because one small sound sets it off. The paradox prepares a poem about sounds that reveal something larger.
evidence: The stilly murmur of the distant Sea Tells us of silence.
Slow saddening round, and mark the star of eve

questions.prompt: How does Coleridge describe the harp’s music? Find a comparison that makes the sound seem alive.
facilitatorNotes: The breeze caresses the lute like a lover; its notes are a “soft floating witchery of sound” like elves voyaging from Fairy-Land, and melodies like birds of Paradise that never land. The images grow wilder and less solid as the music swells, so the verse drifts the way the sound does.
evidence: Such a soft floating witchery of sound
Nor pause, nor perch, hovering on untam'd wing!

questions.prompt: “And what if all of animated nature / Be but organic Harps”? Put this idea in your own words. What plays the part of the breeze?
facilitatorNotes: Every living thing might be an instrument, and thought the music made when one great spirit, “one intellectual breeze,” sweeps over them; that breeze is the soul of each and God of all. The third stanza prepared it: idle thoughts crossed his “passive brain” as gales cross the lute. Readers may find the idea beautiful, or unsettling because it makes minds passive.
evidence: Be but organic Harps diversely fram'd,
At once the Soul of each, and God of all?
Traverse my indolent and passive brain,

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker take back his idea in the last stanza? Do you think he really gives it up?
facilitatorNotes: Sara’s “more serious eye” reproves him, and he calls such thoughts “Bubbles that glitter as they rise and break,” returning to a humble faith and gratitude for peace, home and her. Some readers take the retreat as sincere; others notice that the bold idea got the poem’s most memorable lines, and that the reproof is a look, not an argument.
evidence: But thy more serious eye a mild reproof
Bubbles that glitter as they rise and break

readings.title: France: An Ode
readings.challenge: Track how a speaker’s judgment of a political cause changes from stanza to stanza, and what finally changes it.
readings.focus: Hope, self-deception and disillusion: where liberty can and cannot be found.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). He wrote this ode, a formal poem of address, in February 1798 (the date is printed at the end). In 1789 the French Revolution overthrew the old monarchy in the name of liberty. When the kings of Europe went to war against the new republic in 1792–1793, Britain joined them, and young English radicals such as Coleridge took France’s side. The Reign of Terror (1793–1794) followed, and early in 1798 French armies invaded Switzerland (“Helvetia”), a small republic famous for its free mountain people. “Gratulation” means joyful greeting; to “whelm” is to overwhelm; paeans are songs of triumph; “inexpiable” means unforgivable; “Priestcraft’s harpy minions” are greedy servants of scheming clergy; pinions are wings.
readings.contentNote: The poem describes revolutionary violence and war in images of blood and wounds, and condemns its opponents in harsh religious terms.

excerpt.locator: France: an Ode, the whole poem (stanzas I–V) with its date; opens “Ye Clouds! that far above me float and pause, Whose pathless march no mortal may…”; closes “_February_, 1798.”.

questions.prompt: In stanza I the speaker calls on clouds, waves and woods to “Bear witness” for him. What does he want them to witness, and why choose them?
facilitatorNotes: That he has always worshipped “divinest Liberty.” Clouds, ocean and woods obey only “eternal laws” and no human master, so they are free already and fit witnesses. The last stanza returns to them.
evidence: Whose pathless march no mortal may controul!
The spirit of divinest Liberty.

questions.prompt: When Britain went to war with France, which side did the speaker take, and what did it cost him?
facilitatorNotes: He sang “defeat” to the allied side, though Britain was dear to him through friendships and youthful loves; he “wept at Britain's name.” He claims his loyalty to liberty outranked loyalty to his country. Readers can debate whether that was principled or disloyal.
evidence: Though dear her shores and circling ocean,
And hung my head and wept at Britain's name.

questions.prompt: In stanza III he keeps explaining away bad news from France. What excuses does he make for the Revolution’s violence?
facilitatorNotes: He treats the blasphemy and “drunken passions” as storms hiding a sun that is still rising, scolds his own fears, and predicts that France, “conquering by her happiness alone,” will spread freedom. Note the contradiction in “compel the nations to be free”: forcing freedom on others is already a warning sign.
evidence: The Sun was rising, though ye hid his light!
Shall France compel the nations to be free,

questions.prompt: What finally changes his mind, and where does he find liberty in stanza V? Is this a satisfying answer?
facilitatorNotes: The invasion of peaceful Switzerland: “Forgive me, Freedom!” He concludes that liberty never lives “in forms of human power,” neither in kings nor in revolutions, but is felt in wild nature on a sea-cliff. Some readers find this a wise lesson about trusting political causes; others find it a retreat into private feeling, since liberty is no longer something people can build together.
evidence: Forgive me, Freedom! O forgive those dreams!
Didst breathe thy soul in forms of human power.
O Liberty! my spirit felt thee there.

readings.title: Fears in Solitude
readings.challenge: Hold together a long meditation that moves from a quiet valley to a nation’s faults and back.
readings.focus: Patriotism that criticises its own country, and the distance between the words of war and its reality.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). The subtitle says he wrote this in April 1798, during the alarm of an invasion: Britain was at war with Revolutionary France, and a French army was gathering across the Channel. He signs it from Nether Stowey, where he lived with his wife and baby son near his friend Thomas Poole (the “mansion of my friend”). Furze is gorse, a yellow-flowered shrub; a dell is a small valley; “vernal” means of spring; “perdition” is ruin; perjury is lying under oath, here the oaths that officials had to swear; fratricide is killing one’s brother; “translated” means taken up to heaven without dying; “belike” means perhaps; a beacon is a hilltop signal fire.
readings.contentNote: The poem imagines invasion and the deaths of soldiers and civilians, and accuses Britain of carrying slavery abroad. It calls the French “a light yet cruel race” and speaks of atheism with contempt; these are the speaker’s wartime judgments.

excerpt.locator: Fears in Solitude, written in April 1798, during the alarm of an invasion, the whole poem with its place and date; opens “A green and silent spot, amid the hills, A small and silent dell! O'er stiller place No…”; closes “NETHER STOWEY, _April_ 20, 1798.”.

questions.prompt: What does the dell give the “humble man” in the first verse paragraph, and what breaks into his peace?
facilitatorNotes: Quiet, the unseen lark, “meditative joy,” religious meanings in nature. Then the thought of invasion: such a man “must feel / For all his human brethren.” His peace cannot last because he cannot stop caring about others.
evidence: Oh! 'tis a quiet spirit-healing nook!
For all his human brethren--O my God!

questions.prompt: Instead of blaming the enemy first, the speaker says “We have offended.” Name two wrongs he charges his own country with.
facilitatorNotes: Carrying “slavery and pangs” to distant peoples (the slave trade and empire); oaths sworn everywhere and broken, “one scheme of perjury”; drinking “Pollutions from the brimming cup of wealth”; bored, careless religion. It took courage to say this during an invasion scare.
evidence: And borne to distant tribes slavery and pangs,
All, all make up one scheme of perjury,

questions.prompt: Why does he say the British enjoy war “as a thing to talk of”? What is wrong with their “dainty terms”?
facilitatorNotes: Safe behind fleets and seas, they read about battles at breakfast as entertainment, “Spectators and not combatants.” The smooth words for victories and defeats are “mere abstractions” that hide wounds, pain and widows. Readers may compare how war sounds in news today.
evidence: Spectators and not combatants!
The best amusement for our morning meal!
As if the soldier died without a wound;

questions.prompt: He also calls the French “an impious foe” and urges Britons to drive them back. Does this contradict his criticism of Britain, or fit with it?
facilitatorNotes: It can fit: he wants Britain defended but returning “Not with a drunken triumph, but with fear,” repenting its own wrongs, because true courage dares to look “At their own vices.” Others may argue that “a light yet cruel race” slips into the very war talk he condemns. The return to the dell and to “my babe” suggests what he is really defending.
evidence: Not with a drunken triumph, but with fear,
At their own vices. We have been too long
a light yet cruel race,

readings.title: Love
readings.challenge: Read a story told inside a story, and notice how the inner tale works on its listener.
readings.focus: Courtship through art: a song that says what the singer cannot say directly.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). Love was first printed in a newspaper in 1799 (the date is printed at the end) and was one of his most popular poems in his lifetime. It is a ballad in four-line stanzas. A lay and a ditty are songs; a “burning brand” on a knight’s shield is a flaming torch used as his badge; to “expiate” is to make amends for; “virgin-shame” and “virgin pride” mean a young unmarried woman’s modesty and self-respect; “faultering” is an old spelling of faltering.

excerpt.locator: Love, the whole poem with its date; opens “All thoughts, all passions, all delights, Whatever stirs this mortal frame, All are but…”; closes “1799.”.

questions.prompt: Where are the speaker and Genevieve, and what is he doing? Why might he have chosen this place and this song?
facilitatorNotes: On a hillside by a ruined tower, in moonlight, with Genevieve leaning against the statue of an armed knight. He sings an “old rude song” that suits the ruin, knowing she loves songs “that make her grieve.” Some readers will see a careful plan in his choice.
evidence: She leant against the arméd man,
She loves me best, whene'er I sing The songs that make her grieve.

questions.prompt: Retell the Knight’s story in a few sentences. How is it like the speaker’s own situation, and how is it different?
facilitatorNotes: The Knight woos the Lady for ten years, is driven mad by her scorn, wanders haunted by visions, saves her from a murderous band, and dies sane in her care. Like the speaker, he loves and pleads; unlike him, he wins her pity only when it is too late.
evidence: And that for ten long years he wooed The Lady of the Land.
When on the yellow forest-leaves A dying man he lay;--

questions.prompt: “With which I sang another's love, / Interpreted my own.” What does this mean? Where does the song stop, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Singing the Knight’s love lets him express his own without saying it outright. The song breaks off at the Knight’s dying words, when his “faultering voice and pausing harp” move her more than words could. Readers can decide whether the pause is real emotion, a singer’s art, or both.
evidence: With which I sang another's love, Interpreted my own.
My faultering voice and pausing harp Disturbed her soul with pity!

questions.prompt: The poem opens: “All thoughts, all passions, all delights … / All are but ministers of Love.” How does the story prove this? Is the speaker as innocent as he calls Genevieve?
facilitatorNotes: Music, pity, the evening and the sad tale all end by serving love. He calls her “guileless,” yet he gazes, chooses a grieving song, and admits her embrace was “partly 'twas a bashful art”: both lovers use a little art. Some readers find the poem charming; others find the speaker a little calculating.
evidence: All are but ministers of Love,
'Twas partly love, and partly fear, And partly 'twas a bashful art,

readings.title: Hymn before Sun-rise, in the Vale of Chamouni
readings.challenge: Follow a speaker whose gazing turns into prayer, and weigh what the poem claims to have seen.
readings.focus: A mountain made to speak: questions, commands and paradox in a hymn of praise.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). He wrote this in 1802 (the date is printed at the end). Chamouni, now Chamonix, is the valley below Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in the Alps; the Arve and Arveiron are its rivers. Coleridge never went there: he worked from a short German poem by Friederike Brun and from his own climbs in the English Lake District. The prose headnote is his; the bracket inside it was added by the 1912 editor to record that his journal The Friend (1809) printed “liveliest” where this text has “loveliest.” “Sovran” means sovereign; “ebon” means black as ebony; “amain” means at full speed; a hierarch is a high priest.

excerpt.locator: Hymn before Sun-rise, in the Vale of Chamouni, the whole poem with Coleridge’s prose headnote and date; opens “Besides the Rivers, Arve and Arveiron, which have their sources in the foot of Mont…”; closes “1802.”.

questions.prompt: In the first stanza the speaker gazes at the mountain until it vanishes from his thought. What happens to him, and what happens next?
facilitatorNotes: The dark silent mass seems to pierce the sky; staring, he forgets the mountain and prays to “the Invisible alone.” Then the mountain steals back into his thought “like some sweet beguiling melody” until his soul swells “vast to Heaven.” Looking becomes worship.
evidence: Didst vanish from my thought: entranced in prayer
Yet, like some sweet beguiling melody,

questions.prompt: Many sentences in the middle stanzas begin with “Who.” Why ask so many questions, and who answers them?
facilitatorNotes: They are questions the speaker already knows the answer to, piling up wonder at each feature: the mountain’s base, its light, its torrents. The answer is shouted by the landscape itself: the torrents and ice-plains echo “GOD!” The poem makes nature speak its own hymn.
evidence: Who sank thy sunless pillars deep in Earth?
Answer! and let the ice-plains echo, GOD!

questions.prompt: How can torrents be “Motionless” and cataracts “silent”? What is he describing, and why put it this way?
facilitatorNotes: Glaciers look like waterfalls frozen in mid-plunge, as if stopped by “a mighty voice.” The paradox turns a natural feature into evidence of a commanding creator.
evidence: Motionless torrents! silent cataracts!
And stopped at once amid their maddest plunge!

questions.prompt: Coleridge had never seen Mont Blanc. Does knowing this weaken the poem? Which parts could come from reading and imagination rather than eyewitness?
facilitatorNotes: Some readers feel misled, since the hymn presents itself as a moment of experience (“I gazed upon thee”). Others argue that its real subject is the soul’s response, which he knew from his own mountains. The headnote’s facts about five torrents and the gentian read like a guidebook, and the bold images could come from imagination.
evidence: O dread and silent Mount! I gazed upon thee,
five conspicuous torrents rush down its sides

readings.title: A Christmas Carol
readings.challenge: Notice when the speaker changes and how a Christmas story turns into an argument.
readings.focus: Peace seen from below: Mary’s answer to the glamour of war.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). This carol, dated 1799 at the end, was printed in a newspaper on Christmas Day that year, while Britain was at war with France. It retells the shepherds’ visit to the newborn Jesus in the stable, from the Gospel of Luke, and then gives Mary a speech. “Elate” means joyful and proud; “low estate” means humble position, an echo of Mary’s song in Luke; mail is armour; laurels are victors’ wreaths; a board is a table, so what is on it is the family’s food.

excerpt.locator: A Christmas Carol, the whole poem (stanzas I–VIII) with its date; opens “The shepherds went their hasty way, And found the lowly stable-shed Where the…”; closes “1799.”.

questions.prompt: What do the shepherds tell Mary, and how does she respond? Which detail makes her a real mother rather than a statue?
facilitatorNotes: They tell of the light and the angels’ song, “Glory to God on high! and Peace on Earth.” She presses the baby closer, cries “the Babe is mine!” and feels her milk rush: a bodily joy, not a calm pose.
evidence: And closer still the Babe she pressed;
Joy rose within her, like a summer's morn;

questions.prompt: In stanzas IV and V someone asks Mary questions. What picture of war does this voice offer?
facilitatorNotes: War as “a youthful king,” a hero in armour, hailed by monarchs and loved by maidens: glory and fame. The voice may be the poet testing her, or the common view of the age.
evidence: Didst thou ne'er love to hear of fame and glory?
And is not War a youthful king,

questions.prompt: How does Mary answer? Why does being poor make her glad of peace?
facilitatorNotes: She sends that picture back to the court: she is “a woman poor and mean,” and so she sees war as a ruffian that tears sons from fathers, kills husbands and steals a widow’s earnings. The poor pay for war; the powerful enjoy its glory.
evidence: I am a woman poor and mean,
That from the agéd father tears his child!

questions.prompt: The last line repeats the end of stanza III. What has changed in the meaning of “Peace on Earth” by the end?
facilitatorNotes: At first it is the angels’ message and Mary’s private joy; at the end it is her considered answer to war, “wisely” held. Printed in wartime, the carol also speaks to Britain in 1799. Readers may notice joy “rose” has become joy “rises,” in the present.
evidence: Then wisely is my soul elate,
Joy rises in me, like a summer's morn:

readings.title: The Raven
readings.challenge: Hear the poem in the voice of the boy telling it, and follow one acorn from the pigs’ feast to the shipwreck.
readings.focus: A nursery-tale rhythm carrying a story of grief and revenge.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). This ballad, dated 1797 at the end, was first printed in 1798. Its subtitle presents it as a tale a schoolboy tells the younger children at Christmas, so the jingling rhyme and loose rhythm are part of the joke. Mast is the acorns and nuts that pigs eat from the forest floor; jet is a black stone; Melancholy, gloom, is imagined as a witch; “enow” means enough; “in leathern guise” means dressed in leather; a pent-house is a sloping roof over a door, so the Woodman’s brow juts out; a “hem” is a grunt; a ship “bulged” on a rock when its hull was stove in; fleet means swiftly.
readings.contentNote: The Woodman’s felling kills the Raven’s young, and a shipwreck drowns everyone aboard while the Raven rejoices.

excerpt.locator: The Raven: A Christmas Tale, told by a School-boy to his little Brothers and Sisters, the whole poem with its date; opens “A CHRISTMAS TALE, TOLD BY A SCHOOL-BOY TO HIS LITTLE BROTHERS AND SISTERS”; closes “1797.”.

questions.prompt: The subtitle says a schoolboy is telling this tale to his little brothers and sisters. Find two places where you can hear the boy’s voice. What does he skip, and why?
facilitatorNotes: “I can’t tell half his adventures” skips many years in four lines; “they did say” passes on a rumour; “happy enow” and “See! see!” sound like a storyteller performing for listeners. He hurries past the dull parts to the exciting ones, as children’s storytelling does. Some readers hear Coleridge gently mocking ballad style as well.
evidence: I can't tell half his adventures.
He belonged, they did say, to the witch Melancholy!

questions.prompt: Trace the life of the single acorn the pigs leave behind. What is ironic about the Raven’s part in it?
facilitatorNotes: The Raven buries it beside the river; it becomes the oak where he nests and raises his young; the Woodman fells it, floats it downriver and builds it into a ship. The Raven planted his own home, and the tree he planted becomes the ship whose loss he celebrates.
evidence: He picked up the acorn and buried it straight
And with this tree and others they made a good ship.

questions.prompt: Does the Raven cause the storm? What does the poem say, and what does it leave open?
facilitatorNotes: It never says so: the storm simply rises, “in sight of the land,” while the Raven circles and caws “to the blast.” His tie to “the witch Melancholy” and his feathers that stay dry in rain hint at dark powers, so readers may decide it is magic, fate punishing the Woodman, or chance the Raven enjoys.
evidence: Such a storm there did rise as no ship could withstand.
Round and round flew the raven, and cawed to the blast.

questions.prompt: “They had taken his all, and REVENGE IT WAS SWEET!” Is the Raven’s revenge just? How do you think the poem wants us to take this ending?
facilitatorNotes: His loss is real: his young killed, his mate dead of a broken heart. But the drowned sailors did nothing to him, and he thanks Death for “this treat.” A child may cheer the rough justice; an older reader sees revenge falling on the innocent and grief turned cruel. The capital letters may be the boy’s glee, or Coleridge’s irony at it.
evidence: He heard the last shriek of the perishing souls
And he thank'd him again and again for this treat:

readings.title: To a Young Ass, Its Mother Being Tethered near It
readings.challenge: Decide whether the poem is about a donkey, about poor people, or both, and find the line where it widens.
readings.focus: Pity for an animal that becomes a protest about poverty.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). He wrote this in 1794, when he and the poet Robert Southey were planning a small community in America where all would work and share property equally; critics mocked the poem for calling a donkey “Brother.” The line in single quotation marks is from Hamlet’s speech “To be, or not to be.” Filial means of a child towards a parent; to be “fain” is to wish; a charmer here is a sweetheart; “ribless” means too well fed to show ribs; Fashion means fashionable society.

excerpt.locator: To a Young Ass, its Mother being tethered near it, the whole poem with its date; opens “Poor little Foal of an oppresséd race! I love the languid patience of thy face: And oft…”; closes “1794.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker notice about the foal, and what reasons does he imagine for its sadness?
facilitatorNotes: Its “languid patience,” hanging head and refusal to play, “most unlike” young things. He wonders whether it fears its future or grieves at its mother’s “shorten'd chain.” He reads human feelings into an animal; readers can decide how far that is fair.
evidence: I love the languid patience of thy face:
To see thy wretched mother's shorten'd chain?

questions.prompt: “For much I fear me that He lives like thee, / Half famish'd in a land of Luxury!” How does the poem’s subject widen here?
facilitatorNotes: The donkey’s master is poor and hungry too, in a rich country; his hardness may come from his own misery, and he should have learned pity from shared suffering. The poem turns from an animal to the poor.
evidence: Half famish'd in a land of Luxury!
Pity--best taught by fellowship of Woe!

questions.prompt: The speaker hails the foal as a brother and imagines a dell of “Peace and mild Equality.” Is the poem serious, comic, or both?
facilitatorNotes: It means its hope of equality seriously, but it is full of comic touches: Laughter tickling Plenty’s “ribless side,” a bray sweeter than fashionable music. Coleridge expects scorn and answers it. Some readers find the poem sincere and moving, others absurd; it seems to expect both.
evidence: spite of the fool's scorn!
Of Peace and mild Equality to dwell,
Thy dissonant harsh bray of joy would be,

readings.title: Reflections on Having Left a Place of Retirement
readings.challenge: Follow the poem through three places, the cottage, the hilltop and the world of work, and the argument that moves the speaker from one to the next.
readings.focus: Whether a happy private life is right while others suffer.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). He wrote this about the cottage at Clevedon, near Bristol, where he lived for a few months after his marriage in 1795. The Latin motto from Horace means “more suited to talk” (or prose): this is a plain, conversational poem. A cot is a cottage; Bristowa is Bristol; “viewless” means invisible; seats are country houses; John Howard was a reformer who travelled to relieve prisoners; “vision-weaving” means daydreaming; Science here means knowledge.

excerpt.locator: Reflections on having left a Place of Retirement, the whole poem with its motto and date; opens “Sermoni propriora.--HOR.”; closes “1795.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the cottage “a Blesséd Place”? How does the passing merchant confirm it?
facilitatorNotes: Roses at the window, the sea’s murmur, myrtles and jasmine. A “wealthy son of Commerce” pauses, and the place seems to calm “His thirst of idle gold.” If even he feels it, the place must be blessed; Coleridge may also be gently mocking him.
evidence: Our Myrtles blossom'd; and across the porch
His thirst of idle gold, and made him muse

questions.prompt: From the hilltop the view “seem'd like Omnipresence!” What does he see, and why does it leave no wish in his heart?
facilitatorNotes: Sheep, clouds, river, abbey, hamlets, the Channel and the ocean: the whole world seems pictured in one view, like a temple God built. Wanting nothing, he is content simply to exist.
evidence: It seem'd like Omnipresence!
It was a luxury,--to be!

questions.prompt: Why does he leave? Explain the difference he draws between a “benefactor” and a “brother man.”
facilitatorNotes: He asks whether it was right to dream “On rose-leaf beds” while others toiled and bled. Help given with an unmoved face “chills me while he aids”; real kindness comes with feeling, like Howard’s tear. Yet even cold help beats the pity of those who “sigh for Wretchedness, yet shun the Wretched.”
evidence: While my unnumber'd brethren toil'd and bled,
My benefactor, not my brother man!
Who sigh for Wretchedness, yet shun the Wretched,

questions.prompt: In the last stanza the cottage returns in memory. What does “had none greater! And that all had such!” wish for, and how does the last line answer it?
facilitatorNotes: That no one had a grander home and everyone had one as good: equality in simple comfort. “It might be so—but the time is not yet”: only a future Kingdom will bring it. Readers may find the ending hopeful or resigned.
evidence: Ah!--had none greater! And that all had such!
It might be so--but the time is not yet.

readings.title: To the Rev. George Coleridge
readings.challenge: Compare the two lives the poem sets side by side, the brother’s and the poet’s, and listen for what the poet admits about himself.
readings.focus: A settled life and a wandering one, and thanks to an older brother.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). George Coleridge, his elder brother, was a clergyman and schoolmaster in their home town of Ottery St Mary in Devon and looked after Samuel, the youngest child of the family, after their father died; the subtitle says the poem was sent with a book of poems. The Latin motto from Horace means “known for a father’s spirit towards his brothers.” A manchineel is a tropical tree with poisonous sap; “predestinated wreaths” are crowns of fame he felt meant for him; a sash is a window frame; firstling-lays are first poems; intemperate means unrestrained.

excerpt.locator: To the Rev. George Coleridge of Ottery St. Mary, Devon, the whole poem with its subtitle, motto, place and date; opens “_With some Poems_”; closes “NETHER-STOWEY, SOMERSET, _May_ 26, 1797.”.

questions.prompt: What is the “blesséd lot” of the brother? What details make it seem complete?
facilitatorNotes: He returns after youth’s turmoil to his father’s house and sees his own children climb the lap where he first prayed; the brothers are drawn “to one centre.” Life comes full circle in one place.
evidence: To the same dwelling where his father dwelt;
Hath drawn you to one centre.

questions.prompt: How is the poet’s own fortune different? Explain the two images of friends as trees.
facilitatorNotes: Moved away too young, he has chased “chance-started friendships.” Some friends sheltered him only until a storm, then dropped all their gathered rain on him at once; others, like the poisonous manchineel, tempted him into their shade and poisoned him. Yet he has found lasting shelter: a home, a wife and a child.
evidence: Chasing chance-started friendships.
False and fair-foliag'd as the Manchineel,
Of Husband and of Father

questions.prompt: What did George do for him? Which line sums up their relationship?
facilitatorNotes: George watched his boyhood “with a father's eye,” rebuked his faults and grieved over his troubles in silence. “Lov'd as a brother, as a son rever'd thee!” holds both roles.
evidence: Didst trace my wanderings with a father's eye;
Lov'd as a brother, as a son rever'd thee!

questions.prompt: The poem ends by asking forgiveness in advance. For what, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Some poems may “strike discordant” on George’s milder mind with “error or intemperate truth”; he hopes age will calm them and love forgive. Readers may hear a younger brother’s humility, or a polite defence of views he will not give up.
evidence: Will strike discordant on thy milder mind)
If aught of error or intemperate truth

readings.title: The Dungeon
readings.challenge: Follow an argument in two halves, a prison and a healing nature, and decide what the poem says punishment does to a person.
readings.focus: Prison as a cause of the evil it claims to cure.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). This speech comes from his play Osorio (1797); he printed it on its own as “The Dungeon” in Lyrical Ballads (1798). Mountebanks are quack doctors; “ministrations” are acts of care; distempered means sick in mind; benignant means kindly.

excerpt.locator: The Dungeon, the whole poem with its date (the editor’s bracketed note on its source, which comes before it, is not part of the reading); opens “And this place our forefathers made for man! This is the process of our love and wisdom,…”; closes “1797.”.

questions.prompt: The first line is “And this place our forefathers made for man!” What tone do you hear, and which words in the next lines carry it?
facilitatorNotes: Bitter irony: a cruel place is called “the process of our love and wisdom.” The questions that follow (“Most innocent, perhaps—and what if guilty? / Is this the only cure?”) ask the reader to judge.
evidence: This is the process of our love and wisdom,
Is this the only cure? Merciful God!

questions.prompt: According to the poem, what happens to a prisoner’s “energies”? Explain the image.
facilitatorNotes: Shut off by ignorance and poverty, they “roll back upon his heart,” stagnate and turn to poison; the dungeon then deforms his soul further by sights of more deformity. Prison produces the evil it punishes.
evidence: His energies roll back upon his heart,
Unmoulds its essence, hopelessly deform'd

questions.prompt: How does Nature heal in the second stanza, and how is this cure different from the dungeon’s?
facilitatorNotes: Through colours, sweet smells and the music of woods and waters, until the wanderer cannot bear to be “a jarring and a dissonant thing” and weeps his way back. Nature draws him into harmony; prison isolates him. Students may question whether nature alone could reform an offender; the poem is an argument, not a plan.
evidence: To be a jarring and a dissonant thing,
His angry spirit heal'd and harmoniz'd

readings.title: Written in the Album at Elbingerode, in the Hartz Forest
readings.challenge: Follow the speaker from a mountain view to homesickness, and decide what he says gives a landscape its meaning.
readings.focus: Why the grandest view can leave us cold, and love of country beside a larger home.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). In 1798–99 he studied in Germany; as the date shows, he wrote this in May 1799, after climbing the Brocken, the highest peak of the Harz mountains, in a visitors’ book (album) at Elbingerode. Sovran means supreme; sepulchral means like tombs; a kidling is a young goat; cyphers are figures without meaning; “import” is meaning.

excerpt.locator: Written in the Album at Elbingerode, in the Hartz Forest, the whole poem with its date; opens “I stood on Brocken's sovran height, and saw Woods crowding upon woods, hills over hills,…”; closes “_May_ 17, 1799.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker see and hear on the way down from the Brocken? Why does he move “In low and languid mood”?
facilitatorNotes: Woods upon woods, moss heaped like graves, a hollow birdsong, waterfalls, goats; yet the scene feels empty to him. Outward forms, even the loftiest, take their power from “the Life within”; without it they are “Fair cyphers.”
evidence: Their finer influence from the Life within;--
Fair cyphers else: fair, but of import vague

questions.prompt: What does give a landscape meaning, according to the poem? Name the kinds of “History or prophecy” he lists.
facilitatorNotes: Friend, child, a first love, father, and “our adoréd country”: the people and places we love. A landscape matters when it tells our own story.
evidence: History or prophecy of friend, or child,
Or father, or the venerable name

questions.prompt: His longing for England makes the whole view float away. How does the end of the poem keep that feeling from becoming narrow?
facilitatorNotes: He asks the stranger not to blame these impulses, but also not to doubt the spirit that feels God everywhere, who made mankind “one mighty family” and “the World our Home.” Love of one country sits beside a wider love; readers may debate whether the two fit easily.
evidence: O dear, dear England! how my longing eye
Himself our Father, and the World our Home.

readings.title: Inscription for a Seat by the Road Side Half-way up a Steep Hill Facing South
readings.challenge: Notice who the poem speaks to, and what it asks that reader first to imagine and then to do.
readings.focus: A roadside seat as a lesson in sympathy for the weak.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). Inscriptions, poems written as if cut on a stone or a seat, were a favourite form for Coleridge and Wordsworth around 1800. Sod is turf; a tablet is a stone slab with words cut in it; scantly means scarcely; o'erlaboured means overworked; malady is illness; fervid means hot and eager.

excerpt.locator: Inscription for a Seat by the Road Side half-way up a Steep Hill facing South, the whole poem with its date; opens “Thou who in youthful vigour rich, and light With youthful thoughts dost need no rest! O…”; closes “1800.”.

questions.prompt: Who is “Thou” at the beginning, and why must that person stop?
facilitatorNotes: A young, strong walker for whom valley and hill are equally easy. He must stop because the seat is not for him, and he should think of those who need it.
evidence: Thou who in youthful vigour rich, and light
Glance on this sod, and this rude tablet, stop!

questions.prompt: Name the three kinds of travellers the poem asks the young walker to imagine. What do they have in common?
facilitatorNotes: A foot-worn soldier with his wife, baby and an underfed boy already bound to his father’s trade; a labourer walking home through rain and December cold; the old or sick climbing towards the spring sun. All are poor, tired or weak, and for them the seat is a gift.
evidence: The foot-worn soldier and his family
Who in the spring to meet the warmer sun

questions.prompt: The poem says “Cherish the wholesome sadness!” Why should sadness be wholesome?
facilitatorNotes: Thinking how soon his own strength will wither should make him kinder now: sadness here is not despair but a spur to generosity. Some readers find the turn to death and Heaven heavy for a poem about a bench; others think it fits a hill climbed by the weak.
evidence: Must change to feeble, withered, cold and dry,
Cherish the wholesome sadness!

questions.prompt: What does the poem ask the young reader to do with his strength, and what does it promise in return?
facilitatorNotes: To make his “present strength the staff of all,” a support for others, and so build an inner “seat” for his own old age and death, one “Not built by hands.” The bench becomes a picture of a life of service.
evidence: To make thy present strength the staff of all,
Not built by hands, on which thy inner part,

readings.title: Youth and Age
readings.challenge: Listen to the short refrains (“When I was young!” “Ere I was old!”) and watch the speaker argue with them.
readings.focus: An ageing man refusing, then accepting, that his youth has gone.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). Coleridge worked at this poem for years; the edition dates it 1823–1832. A-maying means celebrating May Day; “this breathing house not built with hands” is the body; the skiffs that need no sail or oar are the new steamboats; a vesper-bell rings for evening prayer; a masker is someone in disguise; “conceit” here means a fanciful idea; “nigh-related” means closely related.

excerpt.locator: Youth and Age, the whole poem with its dates; opens “Verse, a breeze mid blossoms straying, Where Hope clung feeding, like a bee-- Both were…”; closes “1823-1832.”.

questions.prompt: What were Verse and Hope like when the speaker was young? Why does he choose these images?
facilitatorNotes: Verse was a breeze among blossoms and Hope a bee feeding there: light, quick, nourished. Life “went a-maying” with Nature, Hope and Poesy. The images are all spring and easy movement.
evidence: Verse, a breeze mid blossoms straying,
Life went a-maying

questions.prompt: How does the speaker compare his body then and now?
facilitatorNotes: Then it “flashed along” over cliffs and sands like a steamboat that fears no wind or tide; now it is a “breathing house” that “does me grievous wrong,” with silver hair and a drooping walk. Youth and he once lived in it together.
evidence: This body that does me grievous wrong,
When Youth and I lived in't together.

questions.prompt: In the middle he cries “It cannot be that Thou art gone!” What trick does he imagine Youth is playing, and does he believe it?
facilitatorNotes: That Youth is a bold masker in disguise, only pretending to be gone; “Life is but thought,” so he will think Youth is still his house-mate. It is half playful defiance, half self-deception; readers can decide which.
evidence: What strange disguise hast now put on,
That Youth and I are house-mates still.

questions.prompt: The last stanza compares life in old age to a guest. What kind of guest, and what is the effect of the final line?
facilitatorNotes: A poor relation who cannot be rudely sent away, has outstayed his welcome, “And tells the jest without the smile.” The comparison is dry and sad, a joke that is no longer funny, which is the tone of the line itself.
evidence: Like some poor nigh-related guest,
And tells the jest without the smile.

readings.title: Constancy to an Ideal Object
readings.challenge: Work out who “thou” is in this poem, and follow the argument to its surprising last image.
readings.focus: A love that lives only in the mind, and the shadow we make and then follow.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote his best-known poems in 1797–1798, while living at Nether Stowey in Somerset and working closely with William Wordsworth, with whom he published Lyrical Ballads (1798). The date “? 1826” is the editor’s guess. A meed is a reward; a cot is a cottage; a becalmed bark is a ship stuck without wind. The last lines describe a real sight in mountains (sometimes called the Brocken spectre): on a bank of mist, with the sun behind him, a walker may see his own huge shadow with a ring of light around its head.

excerpt.locator: Constancy to an Ideal Object, the whole poem with its date; opens “Since all that beat about in Nature's range, Or veer or vanish; why should'st thou remain…”; closes “? 1826.”.

questions.prompt: Who or what is “thou” in the opening lines? Why is it “The only constant in a world of change”?
facilitatorNotes: A “yearning Thought,” the idea of a beloved that lives only in the brain. Everything real changes or vanishes; only the imagined ideal stays. A constant thought can be a comfort or a torment.
evidence: The only constant in a world of change,
O yearning Thought! that liv'st but in the brain?

questions.prompt: “She is not thou, and only thou art she.” Untangle this line. What gap does it describe?
facilitatorNotes: The real woman is not the ideal; only the ideal is the woman he longs for. He loves an image no living person matches, yet speaks to it as if it stood before him and wishes for “an English home, and thee!”
evidence: She is not thou, and only thou art she,
To have a home, an English home, and thee!

questions.prompt: The poem ends with a woodman who sees “An image with a glory round its head.” What has he really seen, and what does the comparison say about the speaker’s ideal?
facilitatorNotes: His own shadow on the snow-mist, ringed with light; he worships it, not knowing “he makes the shadow, he pursues!” The ideal beloved is likewise the speaker’s own making. Some readers find the ending bleak, since the love is self-made; others find it beautiful, since the mind makes glory.
evidence: An image with a glory round its head;
Nor knows he makes the shadow, he pursues!

readings.title: Easter Holidays
readings.challenge: Follow a schoolboy’s holiday poem as it turns from a day of noisy fun to a lesson about lasting happiness, and judge whether the turn works.
readings.focus: Easter crowds race to a spring fair, and a fourteen-year-old poet asks what kind of joy can last beyond the holiday.
readings.context: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) wrote this poem in 1787, at fourteen, while he was a pupil at Christ’s Hospital, a charity school in London; it stands first in his collected poems. At Easter, Londoners crowded to the holiday fair at Greenwich, downriver on the Thames, by coach and by boat. Festal means festive; feather’d songsters are birds; to confess is to show or acknowledge; the stages are stagecoaches, “breaking” under their loads; a lay is a song; jocund means merry; smarts are pains; variegated means varied; tide here means season. It is read on Easter Sunday.

excerpt.locator: Easter Holidays, the whole poem (verses 1–6) with its date; opens “Hail! festal Easter that dost bring Approach of sweetly-smiling spring, When Nature's…”; closes “1787.”.

questions.prompt: What signs of Easter and spring fill the first three verses, and how do the young holiday-makers spend the day?
facilitatorNotes: Green fields, singing birds and animals feeling “the power of love”; youths crowding the coaches to Greenwich, rowing on the Thames, singing, dancing and shouting until evening. The church festival is joined to the season of spring, and the day is all motion and noise.
evidence: Hail! festal Easter that dost bring
Now youths the breaking stages load

questions.prompt: Where does the poem turn, and what do the joyful young people not think about? Why might a fourteen-year-old write this turn?
facilitatorNotes: At the fourth verse: “But little think their joyous hearts / Of dire Misfortune’s varied smarts,” the sorrows everyone is “born to know.” A moral turn like this was a habit of eighteenth-century verse, so the schoolboy may be imitating the poems he studied; some readers also hear a boy watching the holiday from outside, already aware that it will end.
evidence: But little think their joyous hearts
Which all mankind are born to know

questions.prompt: According to the last two verses, who can stay cheerful “In raging storms or calm serene”? What is the poem’s idea of lasting happiness?
facilitatorNotes: The one who keeps to “Wisdom’s paths” with a firm Virtue that will not weep at misfortune; he finds “Heav’n-born Content.” Happiness that depends on circumstances, like a holiday, ends with the evening; contentment that comes from character does not.
evidence: Yet he who Wisdom's paths shall keep
Heav'n-born Content he still shall find

questions.prompt: The poem ends “Like Easter all the year.” How has the meaning of Easter changed between the first line and the last? Is the ending convincing?
facilitatorNotes: At first Easter is a spring holiday of outings and noise; at the end it stands for an inward joy that can last every day, perhaps touched by the Christian hope the feast celebrates. Some readers find the moral tacked on, and a Virtue that “scorns to weep” rather cold; others admire a young poet trying to make one day’s pleasure last. Strong answers judge the ending against the turn in the fourth verse.
evidence: Like Easter all the year.
